newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia farmers question Clinton trade line.
newsitem.headline: Australia farmers question Clinton trade line.

text.p: Australia's leading rural lobby group the National Farmers' Federation (NFF) said it was not overly impressed by U.S. President Bill Clinton's promises on limited use of rural trade subsidies, noting that just last week the U.S. announced a new dairy export bonus.
NFF executive director Wendy Craik told a weekend conference in Brisbane that Clinton's statement in Australia on rural export subsidies "rang a little hollow".
Earlier last week, the USDA announced a DEIP (Dairy Export Incentive Programme) bonus of A$1,100 a tonne for 500 tonnes of skim milk powder exports to the Philippines, Craik said.
"This led to a A$100.00 a tonne reduction in world prices overnight," she said.
Craik quoted a November 20 Canberra statement by Clinton after Australian Prime Minister John Howard had raised Australian concern over U.S. agricultural export subsidy programmes.

"We are going to do everything we can to make sure that any future use of these programmes is not either directly or indirectly working to the disadvantage of a country that is innocent of any wrongdoing, in this case Australia," Clinton said.
Craik told the Australian Institute of International Affairs in Brisbane: "Now, call us cynics if you may, but NFF refused to be bowled over with gratitude by this statement.

"We have heard this before, and the statements, undoubtedly heartfelt and sincere in concept, rang a little hollow, considering that earlier in the week the USDA announced a (new) DEIP bonus," Craik said.
NFF hoped Bill Clinton would carry through his assurances and show significant leadership on trade, she said.

Craik also urged the Australian government, under Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum commitments, to continue to reduce and eventually eliminate all import barriers, without linkage to tariff changes in other APEC countries.

On the U.S. Farm Bill, which eliminates specific agricultural support programmes and reduces overall trade subsidies, Craik said there was still a long way to go before NFF members' concerns would be appeased.
Sugar and peanuts had escaped fundamental reform, even though pressure continued for the elimination of support programmes.
Fears were also held that a cap of US$701 million between 1996 and 2002 on cotton support may not be effective.
Current dairy price support, to be phased down by the end of 1999 and replaced with a recourse loan programme, may result in a more market-oriented and less supported industry, she said.
"But the bill does not, it appears, contain any provisions which would help Australian access to the U.S. dairy market, boyond the U.S. Uruguay Round commitments," she said.
The main concern was the way the U.S. administers its Export Enhancement Programme (EEP) and DEIP, she said.

"There has been a worrying trend of increased use of DEIP subsidies to Asia, and, if the U.S. decided to reactivate EEP in the future, there is concern that it too will be targeted more into the Asian region," she said.
